L24@P0: Background
L25@P0: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has revolutionized our ability to study cellular diversity by providing high-resolution insights into gene expression at the single-cell
L26@P0: level [1]. With the advancement of scRNA-seq techniques, the volume of single-cell data
L27@P0: across various species, tissues, and developmental stages has expanded significantly,
L28@P0: growing from hundreds of cells to tens of millions [2]. The scRNA-seq data analysis aims
L29@P0: to understand cellular gene expression and functional variations across different diseases
L30@P0: or developmental stages, helping to identify mechanisms underlying cell alterations [3].
L31@P0: Among that, data integration is a critical process for combining data collected from
L32@P0: Abstract
L33@P0: Background Advancements in single-cell RNA sequencing have enabled the analysis
L34@P0: of millions of cells, but integrating such data across samples and methods while
L35@P0: mitigating batch effects remains challenging. Deep learning approaches address this
L36@P0: by learning biologically conserved gene expression representations, yet systematic
L37@P0: benchmarking of loss functions and integration performance is lacking.
L38@P0: Results We evaluate 16 integration methods using a unified variational autoencoder
L39@P0: framework, incorporating batch and cell-type information. Results reveal limitations
L40@P0: in the single-cell integration benchmarking index (scIB) for preserving intra-celltype information. To address this, we introduce a correlation-based loss function and
L41@P0: enhance benchmarking metrics to better capture biological conservation. Using cell
L42@P0: annotations from lung and breast atlases, our approach improves biological signal
L43@P0: preservation. We propose a refined integration framework, scIB-E, and metrics that
L44@P0: provide deeper insights into the integration process and offer guidance for advanced
L45@P0: developments in integrating increasingly complex single-cell data.
L46@P0: Conclusions This benchmark highlights the potential of deep learning-based
L47@P0: approaches for single-cell data integration, emphasizing the importance of biologically
L48@P0: informed metrics and improved benchmarking strategies.

L53@P1: with a similar biological background [4]. However, due to potential data biases, high data
L54@P1: dimension, and sparsity in scRNA-seq data, integrating large-scale single-cell data from
L55@P1: different experiments, studies, and platforms while preserving crucial biological insights
L56@P1: remains a significant challenge [5, 6].
L57@P1: Several statistical methods have been developed to address batch effects in scRNAseq data integration. One strategy is to identify the Mutual Nearest Neighbors (MNN)
L58@P1: of single cells across datasets, including MNN [7], Scanorama [8], and Seurat V3 [9].
L59@P1: Another strategy focuses on balancing cellular neighbors to prevent batch-specific clustering, exemplified by Harmony [10] and batch-balanced k-nearest neighbors (BBKNN)
L60@P1: [11]. Additionally, Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) is employed to identify datasets-shared factors for integration, as seen in LIGER [12]. scMerge [13] and
L61@P1: scMerge2 [14] leverage stably expressed genes or pseudo-replicates to estimate the factor of interest and mitigate unwanted batch variation. While these methods are effective
L62@P1: in aligning and integrating scRNA-seq data, they often encounter difficulties with largescale datasets, particularly those exhibiting high cell-type heterogeneity across datasets
L63@P1: [15].
L64@P1: Deep learning-based approaches have emerged as more powerful and flexible solutions
L65@P1: for single-cell data integration [16]. The capability of deep learning methods in learning large, high-dimensional, and complex datasets advances its ability to obtain crucial
L66@P1: biological variation [17]. Autoencoder is a versatile framework to learn the latent data
L67@P1: representation of high-dimensional single-cell gene expression data. Li et al. developed
L68@P1: the DESC method, which employs an autoencoder to infer unsupervised embedding of
L69@P1: scRNA-seq data and for batch-invariant cell clustering analysis [18]. Another notable
L70@P1: method is single-cell Variational Inference (scVI) [19], a fully probabilistic deep learning
L71@P1: framework that accounts for both biological and technical noise in scRNA-seq data. scVI
L72@P1: uses a conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) framework to treat different batches
L73@P1: as variables while preserving true biological gene expression information. Moreover, the
L74@P1: deep learning framework facilitates more complex model designs and enhances information regularization. The SCALEX method introduces a batch-free encoder to project the batch-invariant embeddings across datasets [20]. Additionally, in atlas-level data
L75@P1: integration, pre-defined cell type information can also be leveraged for data integration.
L76@P1: Single-cell ANnotation using Variational Inference (scANVI) [21] extends scVI by incorporating pre-existing cell state annotations, improving the accuracy of cell type identification in new datasets through a semi-supervised learning approach. Similarly, methods
L77@P1: including scDREAMER [22] and scDML [23] can also utilize predefined cell clustering
L78@P1: information for semi-supervised batch-removal data integration.
L79@P1: The success of deep learning methods in single-cell data batch correction and integration largely depends on the design of the loss function. Generally, the objective of these
L80@P1: methods is to remove unwanted batch effects while preserving biological information
L81@P1: across single-cell datasets. Both batch effects and biological signals can be partially captured by batch labels and predefined cell-type labels, respectively. To address batch correction, techniques such as adversarial learning [22, 24] and information-constraining
L82@P1: [25] methods are employed to minimize batch-specific information across datasets. For
L83@P1: preserving biological information, strategies like supervised domain adaptation [26] and
L84@P1-2: deep metric learning [23] are utilized to ensure cell-type label information is maintained Yi et al. Genome Biology (2025) 26:398 Page 3 of 31
L85@P2: in the integrated data. While various loss function designs are effective in different
L86@P2: methods, a horizontal comparison of the impact of distinct loss function combinations
L87@P2: in single-cell data integration tasks is lacking. Additionally, in the context of single-cell
L88@P2: integration performance benchmarking, the single-cell integration benchmarking (scIB)
L89@P2: [27] framework primarily evaluates methods in two key areas: batch correction and
L90@P2: biological conservation, based on the batch and cell-type labels. While scIB provides a
L91@P2: robust foundation for performance evaluation, it falls short in fully capturing unsupervised intra-cell-type variation. As deep learning models continue to evolve, there is a
L92@P2: growing need for more refined benchmarking metrics that can accurately assess both
L93@P2: batch effect correction and the preservation of critical biological information.
L94@P2: In this study, we developed 16 deep-learning single-cell integration methods across
L95@P2: three distinct levels within a unified variational autoencoder framework. These methods
L96@P2: were designed to comprehensively evaluate the impact of different loss function combinations on data integration, utilizing batch information, cell-type information, or both
L97@P2: jointly. By analyzing the effects of batch correction and biological conservation across
L98@P2: varying loss function configurations, we identified that current benchmarking metrics
L99@P2: and batch-correction methods fail to adequately capture intra-cell-type biological conservation. This finding was validated with multi-layered annotations from the Human
L100@P2: Lung Cell Atlas (HLCA) [28] and the Human Fetal Lung Cell Atlas [29]. To address this
L101@P2: gap, we introduced a correlation-based loss function to better preserve biological signals and refined existing benchmarking metrics by incorporating intra-cell-type biological conservation. We further validated this result with a differential abundance analysis
L102@P2: of the integrated single-cell data. Our findings highlight the potential of deep learning
L103@P2: methods for single-cell data integration, with the refined framework and benchmarking
L104@P2: metrics offering deeper insights into the integration process. These advancements are
L105@P2: poised to drive the development of deep learning methods for integrating increasingly
L106@P2: complex multimodal and spatiotemporal single-cell data.
L107@P2: Results
L108@P2: Deep-learning-based integration of single-cell data
L109@P2: Single-cell data integration is essential for atlas-level single-cell data analysis, and the
L110@P2: advent of deep learning methods has broadened the application of data integration,
L111@P2: enabling a deeper understanding of diverse biological processes. In this study, we present a unified benchmarking framework that evaluates different loss function designs
L112@P2: and information regularization strategies for the data integration task (Fig. 1A, B). We
L113@P2: also reorganize existing benchmarking metrics and expand their applications to include
L114@P2: batch correction and biological conservation at both inter-cell-type and intra-cell-type
L115@P2: levels (Fig. 1C). Additionally, we validate our extended single-cell integration benchmarking (scIB-E) metrics with multi-layer cell annotations and developmental singlecell atlases. Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of our framework by designing and
L116@P2: validating a novel loss function specifically aimed at preserving intra-cell-type biological
L117@P2: structure, as confirmed by differential abundance testing (Fig. 1D).
L118@P2: In this study, we used the scVI [19] and scANVI [21] models as the foundational deeplearning framework to evaluate the effectiveness of different loss function designs and
L119@P2: regularization modules for single-cell data integration. Both methods utilize conditional
L120@P2-3: variational autoencoders to embed single-cell gene expression data, with batch labels of Yi et al. Genome Biology (2025) 26:398 Page 4 of 31
L121@P3: single-cell samples as conditional variables to remove batch effects. In scANVI, known
L122@P3: cell-type labels are incorporated for semi-supervised data integration, enabling the preservation of biological information. Consequently, we applied both batch labels of singlecell samples and known cell-type labels of single cells as the proxies of both batch effects
L123@P3: and biological information, respectively. Thereby, we developed a multi-level deeplearning strategy for single-cell data integration (Fig. 1B). Level-1 focuses on batch effect
L124@P3: removal using batch labels, level-2 incorporates single-cell cell-type labels as biological
L125@P3: conservation restraint, and level-3 integrates both batch and cell-type information for
L126@P3: data integration. Overall, we designed 16 data integration methods based on the scVI
L127@P3: framework across three levels, with the scVI method serving as the baseline for level-1,
L128@P3: and the scANVI method as the baseline for level-2 and − 3.

L138@P3: (CellSupcon) [33], Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) [34], and Domain meta-learning
L139@P3: [35] (Methods). In level-3 methods, we integrated both batch labels and cell-type labels

L163@P4: Assessing intra-cell-type biological information in data integration

L167@P4: information regularization, we applied the CellSupcon [33] loss function with varying
L168@P4: hyperparameters (0, 10, 50, and 100), simulating the absence and increasing intensities

L175@P4: performance.

L209@P7: Correlation-based loss function for comprehensive biological conservation
L210@P7: The biological conservation metrics used in scIB are heavily dependent on pre-annotated cell-type labels. However, the PCR comparison-cell index revealed an opposite
L211@P7: trend concerning these biological conservation metrics. This led us to hypothesize that
L212@P7: the metrics might inadequately capture intra-cell-type biological variation, as they rely
L213@P7: solely on the pre-annotated cell-type labels. The intra-cell-type biological variation
L214@P7: reflects cellular diversity within annotated populations, encompassing potentially significant biological signals related to micro-populations or disease-specific subtypes.
L215@P7: To confirm that, we utilized a multi-layer annotated single-cell lung atlas featuring
L216@P7: five levels of cellular annotations [28], ranging from broad cell populations to the finest
L217@P7: resolved subsets. This framework allowed us to examine single-cell biological information at varying scales. Using the level-1 cell-type labels for model training, we assessed
L218@P7: scIB indices across different methods with varying CellSupcon weights. To quantify the
L219@P7: conservation of intra-cell-type biological variation, we analyzed the changes in scIB
L220@P7: indices across cell annotation levels. Our findings revealed consistent trends in the batch
L221@P7: correction index with varying CellSupcon weights across annotation levels (Fig. 4A).
L222@P7: However, the biological conservation indices varied across cell levels, suggesting that
L223@P7: current biological conservation metrics fail to fully capture cellular biological diversity
L224@P7: (Fig. 4A and Additional file 2: Table S7).

L227@P7: of single cells before and after data integration within each batch (Methods). Biological
